claims.text: The overall high-temperature wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings is governed primarily by the formation and stability of protective surface oxide layers.
Increasing substrate temperature during deposition promotes formation of protective oxide layers during subsequent high-temperature wear.
Higher deposition temperatures produce finer grains in FeNiCrCoCu coatings.
Higher deposition temperatures enhance elemental homogeneity in FeNiCrCoCu coatings.
Finer grains facilitate development of adherent, continuous oxide layers during high-temperature wear.
Greater elemental homogeneity facilitates development of adherent, continuous oxide layers during high-temperature wear.
Continuous, adherent oxide layers reduce the wear rate of FeNiCrCoCu coatings.
Higher deposition temperatures promote stable protective oxides such as Cr2O3 and NiO during high-temperature wear.
The protective oxides reduce direct metal-to-metal contact.
Reducing direct metal-to-metal contact minimizes material loss.
A FeNiCrCoCu coating deposited at approximately 400°C will have a lower high-temperature wear rate than a coating deposited at room temperature.
A FeNiCrCoCu coating deposited at approximately 400°C will exhibit less material loss than a room-temperature-deposited coating under identical wear conditions.
The wear improvement will be most pronounced between 500°C and 800°C because oxide formation is thermodynamically favored in that range.
The proposed mechanism applies to FeNiCrCoCu coatings on conventional metal substrates under moderate to high loads at 500–800°C.
The proposed mechanism does not apply outside 500–800°C or to bulk FeNiCrCoCu alloys.
Prior studies focused mainly on room-temperature wear or bulk alloys rather than deposition-temperature effects on high-temperature coating wear.
